newsitem.title: UK: Czech crown crisis dulls investors' risk appetite.
newsitem.headline: Czech crown crisis dulls investors' risk appetite.

text.p: The Czech crown's sickness is likely to blunt investors' general appetite for risk, but other countries' healthier economic fundamentals should shield their currencies from serious infection, analysts said on Tuesday.

"Quite often we see a contagion that goes well beyond any economic linkages. It's partly a degree of risk aversion that investors adopt after negative news," said Avinash Persaud, head of currency research at JP Morgan.
The Slovak crown, Polish zloty, Hungarian forint and Greek drachma all weakened in the Czech crown's wake on Tuesday.

The Czech central bank on Monday allowed the crown to float, in its latest attempt to staunch a tide of heavy selling. The crown promptly tumbled to a rate implying 11.78 percent below parity in its now defunct mark/dollar basket.

The Czechs had used interest rate hikes, official intervention and restraints on foreigners' money market access to fight a speculative assault triggered largely by market concerns over bloated current account deficits.
Similar worries earlier sparked a run on the Thai baht. But Hungary and Poland do not share such problems, analysts said.
"Our view is that it's a psychological thing, at least for Poland and Hungary," said Sara Zervos, emerging markets strategist at BZW.
"The fundamentals are absolutely fine, they don't have big current account deficits, and they don't have the external problems that the Czech Republic has," she added.
Moreover, Poland is not so reliant on the vagaries of speculative flows.

"They don't have anywhere near the kind of foreign hot money that has driven the Czech crown to such overvalued levels and then led to the reversal this week," said Peter von Maydell, senior currency economist at UBS.
The Slovak crown -- inextricably linked as it is with its Czech namesake -- is another story.

"There's a very strong link between the Czech and Slovak crowns still -- that is a natural target for the next speculative attack," said Susanne Hallergard, East European economist at ING Barings in London.

Though access to Slovak markets is very limited, analysts said the Slovak crown will suffer since the Czech is now much cheaper on a relative price basis. That means Slovakia risks running a huge deficit with the Czech Republic, from which it split in 1993.
In time, that will mean Slovakia will be forced either to change its exchange regime as the Czechs have done, or to devalue, said Hallergard.
The Slovak central bank said on Tuesday that no steps were needed in reaction to the Czech crown's fall, which it said posed no threat to Czech-Slovak trade.
Be that as it may, it is not only the Czech Republic's neighbours who are keeping a close watch on developments there.
"Some investors have lost money in Czech so they're less prepared to expose capital and risk to other markets," said JP Morgan's Persaud.
"You may see a degree of risk aversion which may well extend even beyond eastern Europe towards east Asia -- Thailand, the Philippines, Malaysia, and even the South African rand."
The rand is a soft target for speculators as South Africa has very low reserves, as well as question marks over its economic health, analysts said.
The Philippines and Malaysia suffer from current account deficits and weak equity markets -- though where economic growth is slowing in the former, it is strong in the latter, said Persaud.
Even Thailand, which has stemmed the tide of speculative baht selling, is not out of the woods yet.
"Thailand may be able to delay a devaluation," said Persaud. "But it might not avoid it."
